branchingScenario.title: AI Training Data Ethics: The FinFlow Dilemma

startScreen.startScreenTitle: AI Training Data Ethics: The FinFlow Dilemma
startScreen.startScreenSubtitle: As a Product Manager at FinFlow, you uncover a serious data privacy issue. Make choices to navigate this ethical dilemma and shape the outcome.

endScreens.endScreenSubtitle: You chose integrity over expedience. By prioritizing user consent and regulatory compliance, you've built a foundation for sustainable innovation. FinFlow's users can trust that their data is in responsible hands. This is the mark of true ethical leadership.
You balanced competing priorities but left some risks unresolved. A more decisive ethical stance could have reduced regulatory exposure. Reflect on where you compromised — was the trade-off worth it?

Short-term gains have created long-term consequences. By approving data use without consent and withholding findings from regulators, FinFlow now faces significant legal and reputational risk. GDPR fines can reach 4% of global revenue — for FinFlow, that's over $10 million.

params.text:
FinFlow HQ — Sprint Review Room

The data science team beams with pride as they demo their new AI recommendation engine. The projection screen shows impressive metrics — 23% uplift in user engagement, 18% increase in transaction volume.

Then the lead engineer drops a bombshell: "We trained it on three years of real customer transaction data."

Your stomach drops. No one mentioned data consent in any of the sprint reviews. Two million users' financial data has been used without their knowledge.

The room falls silent, waiting for your response.

branchingQuestion.question:
You're a Product Manager at FinFlow, a fintech app with 2M users. During a sprint review, the data science team proudly demos their new AI recommendation engine.

'We trained it on 3 years of real customer transaction data.'

What's your first reaction?

alternatives.text: Challenge: 'Where did this data come from? Was there explicit consent?'

feedback.subtitle: You prioritize transparency. Asking about consent is the first step to ethical data governance.

alternatives.text: Escalate: 'I'm pausing this. Legal needs to review immediately.'

feedback.subtitle: You prioritize compliance over speed. Legal will give you a clearer picture of the risks.

alternatives.text: Approve: 'Great work! Let's plan the production launch.'

feedback.subtitle: Approving without checking consent exposes the company to significant liability under GDPR.

params.text:
Data Science Team Room

You've called an urgent meeting with the data science team. The atmosphere is tense. They clearly thought they were doing something innovative, not something wrong.

The lead engineer pushes back: "Everyone does this — it's just transactional data, not PII. We didn't think we needed consent. Look at what the big tech companies do."

A few team members nod in agreement. Others look uncomfortable. The room is divided and they're all looking to you for direction.

branchingQuestion.question:
The team responds:

'Everyone does this — it's just transactional data, not PII. We didn't think we needed consent.'

How do you handle this pushback?

alternatives.text: Stand firm: 'Under GDPR, transaction data linked to user accounts IS personal data.'

feedback.subtitle: Correct. Transaction data tied to identities is PII under GDPR Article 4(1). You're on solid legal ground.

alternatives.text: Compromise: 'Let's anonymize the data and move forward.'

feedback.subtitle: Anonymization helps, but you still need a lawful basis for processing. Check with Legal first.

alternatives.text: Back down: 'Fine, just be more careful next time.'

feedback.subtitle: This puts everyone at risk. As a manager, you have a duty to intervene when you spot compliance issues.

params.text:
Legal Department — 48 Hours Later

After escalating, you're sitting across from FinFlow's General Counsel. The preliminary legal review is complete, and the verdict is stark.

She slides a document across the table: "This is a clear violation of GDPR Article 6 and CCPA Section 1798.100. No consent was obtained, no Data Protection Impact Assessment was conducted. We have potential exposure to fines of up to 4% of global revenue."

For FinFlow, that's over $10 million. And that's before any civil lawsuits from affected users.

branchingQuestion.question:
You escalate to Legal. After two days, they confirm:

'This is a clear violation of GDPR Article 6 and CCPA Section 1798.100. No consent was obtained, no DPIA conducted.'

What's your next step?

alternatives.text: Self-report to the regulator immediately and halt all data processing

feedback.subtitle: Self-reporting can mitigate penalties under GDPR Article 83. Regulators reduce fines for proactive disclosure.

alternatives.text: Design a retroactive remediation plan with Legal

feedback.subtitle: A remediation plan shows good faith. Ensure it's thorough and timely to satisfy regulatory requirements.

alternatives.text: Quietly stop using the data and hope no one notices

feedback.subtitle: If discovered later, the company faces higher penalties and severe reputational damage. Transparency is safer.

params.text:
Social Media Crisis

Despite your internal efforts, word has gotten out. A prominent FinFlow user — a privacy advocate with 50,000 followers — has posted a screenshot of the AI feature with a damning caption.

Her tweet reads: '@FinFlow, how is my transaction data being used without my consent? I never agreed to this. Is this legal?'

The post is gaining traction. Journalists are starting to ask questions. Your phone hasn't stopped buzzing for the last hour.

branchingQuestion.question:
The beta launches strong. But then a prominent user tweets:

'@FinFlow, how is my transaction data being used without my consent? I never agreed to this.'

The post is gaining traction. How do you respond?

alternatives.text: Pause beta, investigate, and issue a public holding statement

feedback.subtitle: Correct. Acknowledge, pause, investigate. This limits reputational damage and shows good-faith response.

alternatives.text: Respond to the user directly offering an opt-out

feedback.subtitle: Individual responses won't fix the systemic consent issue. A broader pause is needed for true resolution.

alternatives.text: Ignore the tweet — it will blow over

feedback.subtitle: Ignoring complaints often escalates the crisis. Social media amplifies silence into reputational disaster.

params.text:
Back in the Development Pod

Data processing has been paused. The team is restless — they've been told to halt all AI development until the consent issue is resolved.

The lead engineer approaches you with a proposal: 'We could use synthetic data to keep development moving. Generated datasets that mirror real patterns without containing any actual customer information. We'd still need to sort out the legal framework for production, but at least we won't lose momentum.'

Synthetic data is privacy-safe by design — no real user data involved. But it also means you're still proceeding without a proper data governance framework in place.

branchingQuestion.question:
Your principled stand has paused data processing. The team asks:

'Can we use synthetic data to keep development moving while Legal figures out consent?'

What's your call?

alternatives.text: Yes — synthetic data is fine, but require full DPIA documentation

feedback.subtitle: Synthetic data is privacy-safe. Requiring DPIA ensures proper governance going forward.

alternatives.text: No — stop all AI development until we have a data governance framework

feedback.subtitle: A total halt is safe but may be overly cautious. Consider allowing sandboxed work with clear boundaries.

alternatives.text: Yes — go ahead without DPIA. We'll sort out paperwork later

feedback.subtitle: Going ahead without DPIA repeats the original error. The whole point was to fix the broken process.

params.text:
ICO Correspondence — Day 1 of 30

The Information Commissioner's Office has formally acknowledged your self-report. The response is measured but firm.

'You are required to submit a full remediation plan within 30 calendar days. This must include: a Data Protection Impact Assessment, a user notification strategy, a data governance policy, and evidence of board-level oversight.'

Your team is already stretched thin maintaining the existing platform. Finding the bandwidth to meet this deadline will be a real challenge.

branchingQuestion.question:
The ICO acknowledges your report. They give you 30 days to submit a full remediation plan with DPIA, user notification strategy, and data governance policy.

Your team is stretched thin. How do you proceed?

alternatives.text: Dedicate full resources: pull engineers from other projects to meet the deadline

feedback.subtitle: Full resource allocation shows the regulator you're serious. Right call for a high-risk compliance situation.

alternatives.text: Request an extension from the ICO while assembling a cross-functional working group

feedback.subtitle: Extensions are sometimes granted when you show good faith. Use the time to do it right.

alternatives.text: Submit a minimal plan and hope it passes initial review

feedback.subtitle: A weak plan risks enforcement actions. The ICO expects thoroughness and genuine commitment.

params.text:
Internal Investigation — The Full Picture

As part of your remediation planning, you commission a thorough audit of all data used in the AI training pipeline. What comes back is worse than you expected.

The training dataset doesn't just include transaction records. It also contains support chat logs — years of customer service conversations with names, addresses, phone numbers, and account details. Someone on the engineering team thought more data would make the AI smarter.

This escalates the severity from a compliance violation to a full data breach with PII exposure.

branchingQuestion.question:
Your internal investigation reveals something worse: the training dataset includes support chat logs containing names, addresses, and phone numbers. This escalates severity significantly.

What now?

alternatives.text: Expand scope: notify affected users, update regulator, commission full forensic audit

feedback.subtitle: This is the gold standard for data breach response. Full disclosure aligns with ICO guidelines.

alternatives.text: Delete chat log data from training set, report only the original issue

feedback.subtitle: Selective reporting violates your regulatory duty. If discovered, all trust and credibility are destroyed.

alternatives.text: Keep it internal — chat logs weren't the main issue

feedback.subtitle: Withholding material findings is unethical and likely illegal under breach notification laws. Never hide.

params.text:
Data Protection Impact Assessment — Complete

After weeks of intensive work, the DPIA is finally complete. The findings are nuanced:

'Moderate risk to data subjects. Technical and organisational controls are assessed as adequate for data security. However, the legal basis for processing is insufficient and must be remediated.'

The DPIA team presents three remediation pathways. Each has different implications for user trust, regulatory risk, and business continuity. The board is waiting for your recommendation.

branchingQuestion.question:
The Data Protection Impact Assessment is complete. It finds:

'Moderate risk to data subjects. Technical controls are adequate but the legal basis is insufficient.'

Three options are presented. Which do you choose?

alternatives.text: Retrospective consent campaign: email users, explain, ask for opt-in

feedback.subtitle: Retrospective consent respects user autonomy. This aligns with GDPR's transparency principle.

alternatives.text: Legitimate interest argument: document that AI serves user needs, outweighing privacy impact

feedback.subtitle: Legitimate interest is hard to argue when processing was done without any notice at all. Risky.

alternatives.text: Add a line to the privacy policy and move on

feedback.subtitle: A privacy policy line alone doesn't meet GDPR's requirement for specific, informed consent. Inadequate.

params.text:
The Executive Boardroom

You're standing at the head of the boardroom table. The full executive team is here — CEO, CFO, CTO, Chief Legal Officer, Head of Communications. The air is thick with tension.

The CEO breaks the silence: 'This AI could add $5M to our annual recurring revenue. I need you to walk me through the cost-benefit analysis of our options — what's the business case for each path forward?'

All eyes are on you. This is your moment to define FinFlow's ethical stance.

branchingQuestion.question:
You present your findings to the executive board. The CEO asks:

'This AI could add $5M ARR. What's the cost-benefit of our options?'

How do you frame your recommendation?

alternatives.text: Ethical foundation: 'User trust is priceless. Full consent campaign — even if it delays revenue.'

feedback.subtitle: Strong ethical leadership. Delayed but sustainable revenue is worth more than short-term gains with legal risk.

alternatives.text: Balanced: 'Consent campaign but keep the AI model running. If users opt in, great. If not, we pivot.'

feedback.subtitle: Running the model in parallel carries ongoing risk. The regulator may view this as continuing the violation.

alternatives.text: Business-first: '$5M ARR is too big to delay. Accept regulatory risk and launch with a fine budget.'

feedback.subtitle: GDPR fines can reach 4% of global revenue. For FinFlow, that could exceed $10M. The math doesn't work.
